newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan could have headache over scandal penalties.
newsitem.headline: Japan could have headache over scandal penalties.

text.p: Japanese authorities could have more to worry about than making the punishment fit the crime when they finally decide on penalties for financial firms involved in a high-profile racketeer payoff scandal.
Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka admitted on Tuesday to suffering a major headache over how to punish Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank over the scandal without hurting the big bank's customers.
"This is an important point to consider when we are dealing severely with the bank. I am agonising about how to keep the balance," Mitsuzuka told a regular news conference.
And financial experts say the ministry could have another big problem on its plate should allegations of involvement by three more top brokerages besides Nomura Securities prove true.

"I'm sure that the suspension of several large brokerages' business could have negative fallout for the market, but I can't believe that the Finance Ministry and other regulators wouldn't consider those factors when considering what type of penalties to impose," said Walter Alterr, financial analyst at Jardine Fleming Securities.

A lawyer for Ryuichi Koike, the "sokaiya" racketeer at the heart of the scandal which has already led to more than a dozen arrests of officials from DKB and Nomura, said Koike had told prosecutors that the other three of Japan's Big Four brokerages conducted illegal discretionary stock deals for him.

Brokerages are banned from conducting discretionary deals for customers but such deals only become the subject of criminal charges if they are used to illegally compensate clients for losses, the lawyer, Kyuzaburo Hino, told Reuters.
Spokesmen for the three firms said on Tuesday they could not confirm whether Koike had accounts at their brokerages.

A Japan Securities Dealers' Association (JSDA) executive told a news conference on Tuesday that the body had received reports from the three brokerages' compliance sections stating they had not, at this stage, uncovered any illegal activities.

Concern over prospects that the scandal would widen, however, helped slice more than two percent off the Tokyo stock market's 225-share Nikkei average, which closed down 429.44 points at 20,175.42 on Tuesday.
Authorities have taken a tough public stance towards the latest corporate misdeeds, which they fear could cast doubt on the credibility of planned "Big Bang" financial reforms.

Market sources had initially speculated that Nomura's punishment, which they said might be announced as early as next week and take effect a month later, would include suspension of some business such as own-account trading for up to six months.
Punishing all the Big Four at once, however, would have a serious impact on institutional investors.

"If all the Big Four were ordered to suspend business simultaneously, there would be a big impact on institutional investors' basket trades," said a fund manager at a Japanese life insurer, adding that foreign and second-tier brokerages were unable to handle such orders over one billion yen ($8.6 million).
The result, therefore, could be lighter punishment for everyone -- including Nomura.

"They could specify penalties that might sound severe but not have that much impact on liquidity," one analyst said. "The logical assumption is the penalties perforce would be towards the soft end of the market expectations." ($1=115 yen)
